In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened.﴾

Commentary on Surah al-Jinn

It is Meccan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened.﴾ The occasion of revelation of this verse is what Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: that the Prophet set out with some of his companions intending the market of 'Ukaz, and he passed by a palm grove. The devils had been prevented from the heaven, and shooting stars were sent against them. They said to their people: "We have been cut off from news of the heaven." They said: "This is only because of some matter that has occurred on the earth."

It is also narrated that they said this to Iblis, and that Iblis said to them: "Travel through the east and west of the earth so that you may learn what matter has occurred." So a group of them went toward Tihama and saw the Prophet leading his companions in the dawn prayer at Batn Nakhla, and he was reciting the Qur'an. They said: "This is the matter that has occurred." They returned to their people and informed them of that, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Al-Bukhari, in the Sahih, narrated something similar from the narration of Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Jurayj mentioned in his tafsir, from Abu 'Ubayda ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, from Ibn Mas'ud, that the Prophet set out to the jinn to recite the Qur'an to them and call them to Allah. He said to his companions: "Who will accompany me from among you?" In another narration: "Let there stand with me a man who has in his heart not an atom's weight of arrogance."

The people were silent.

He said it a second and a third time, and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud stood up. Ibn Mas'ud said: "I went with the Messenger of Allah before al-Hajun until we entered the valley of Abu Dubb. He said: 'He drew a line for me and said: Do not leave this line.' And the jinn descended upon him like locusts."

He said: He recited the Qur'an to them and raised his voice, and they clung to the ground until I could no longer see them. In another narration, they said to him: "What are you? What are you?" He said: "A prophet."

They said: "Who will bear witness for you?" He said: "This tree." He called the tree, and it came dragging its roots, making a rattling sound, and the tree bore witness to his prophethood, then returned to its place. And in this report: they asked him for provisions, so he gave them bones and dung. They would find the bone fuller of meat than it had been, and the dung was fodder for their animals. The Messenger then forbade istinja' (cleansing) with bone and dung.

A group of the scholars of tafsir said: the affair of the jinn occurred twice, once in Mecca and once at Batn Nakhla. What Ibn 'Abbas narrated is that which occurred at Batn Nakhla, and what Ibn Mas'ud narrated is that which occurred in Mecca. As for that at Batn Nakhla, they passed by the Prophet and listened to the Qur'an. As for that in Mecca, the Messenger set out to them, recited the Qur'an to them, and called them to faith. This is the reconciliation of the two narrations.

It is narrated that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud saw in Iraq a group of the Zutt, and he said: "They resemble the jinn on the night of the jinn."

In a narration from 'Alqama: he said to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "Was there anyone with you with the Messenger of Allah on the night of the jinn?" He said: "No, none of us witnessed it." And he related a report that Muslim mentioned in his book.

There is much difference in the narrations on this matter, and what we have mentioned is the abridged form of them. It is possible that Ibn Mas'ud was with the Messenger of Allah on the night of the jinn, but that he was not with him at the time of the address to the jinn and the recitation of the Qur'an to them. He narrated that he said: "The Messenger of Allah drew a line for me and said: Do not leave this line, and he went off into the mountain. I heard a loud noise and a great sound, and I wanted to go after him, but I remembered the Messenger's saying: Do not leave the line, so I did not go. When he returned, I mentioned that to him, and he said to me: 'Had you left the line, you would never have seen me.'"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "Nafar" is a term for what lies between three and ten.

Ibn al-Sikkit also related this from Ibn Zayd.

They say: "ten nafar," and they do not say "twenty nafar" or "thirty nafar."

It is narrated that they were nine men, and they mentioned their names, and we have explained this.

'Asim narrated from Zirr that among them was Zawba'a.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they said: Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an.﴾ That is: wondrous in its arrangement, its composition, and the soundness of its meaning. And the saying ﴿innā sami'nā﴾ is only correct with a kasra (إِنَّا).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 2:

His words: ﴿It guides to righteousness﴾, meaning: to what is correct and the path of truth.

And His words, exalted is He: ﴿So we believed in it, and we will not associate anyone with our Lord﴾, meaning: we will not make anyone of His creation a partner to Him.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 3:

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord﴾ has been recited with a kasra (i.e., "wa-annahu") and with a fatha ("wa-annahu" read as "wa-anna"). Whoever recites with the kasra, then it is [a continuation of] what the jinn said. Whoever recites with the fatha, then he makes it accusative on the meaning: "We believed that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord," so it is governed by the verb of belief falling upon it. The recitation with the kasra is the better of the two recitations.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿jadd rabbina﴾ means: the greatness (ʿazama) of our Lord. This is the view of Qatada and others.

Al-Jadd (الجد) means greatness (al-ʿazama), and it also means fortune (al-bakht), and it is the father of the father (abu al-ab).

In the hadith of Anas: "When one of us would recite al-Baqara and Al ʿImran, he would become great (jadda) among us," i.e., he would become greatly esteemed [among us].

His, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "The possessor of fortune (dhu al-jadd) will not benefit from you through his fortune," means: the possessor of fortune will not benefit from you through his fortune if you intend by it evil or something disliked.

From al-Hasan, who said: "Exalted is the jadd of our Lord," meaning: exalted is the wealth (ghina) of our Lord.

From Ibrahim and al-Suddi, who both said: "Jadd rabbina" means: the command (amr) of our Lord.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿He has not taken a consort nor a child﴾ means: a wife and a child.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And that our foolish one used to speak about Allah an outrageous lie.﴾ Concerning this there are two views. The first: the "foolish one" is Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him, and this is the view of Mujahid. The second: that it refers to every rebellious disobedient one among the jinn.

As for His words ﴿shatatan﴾ (outrageous), it means: a lie.

It has also been said: injustice.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 5:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And we thought that mankind and the jinn would never speak a lie against Allah﴾. Ya'qub read: "أَن لن تَقول الْإِنْس وَالْجِنّ" (anna lan taqūla al-insu wal-jinnu), meaning "that they would not say." Its meaning is clear. It is as though they thought that whoever spoke something against Allah would be as he said, and that lying against Allah would not be recompensed (yujza).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 6:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that there were men among mankind﴾ If someone says: this whole passage has been read with the accusative (naṣb), so what is the reason for the accusative in it? The answer to this: We have already explained the reason for the accusative in what came before, and the remaining verses were put in the accusative by virtue of adjacency (mujāwara) and coordination (ʿaṭf), or by supposing an implied verb such as "we believed" (āmannā), "we thought" (ẓanannā), or "we bore witness" (shahidnā). The Arabs sometimes make one word follow another in its case-ending purely by adjacency and coordination, as in their saying: "juḥr ḍabb kharib" (the hole of a lizard, which is ruined).

As for His saying ﴿they used to seek refuge with men of the jinn﴾, the explanation in the exegesis is that a man would travel, and the people would travel too, and when they reached a desolate place of the wilderness and nightfall came, they would say: "We seek refuge with the lord of this valley from the foolish ones of his people."

He related from one of them, who is al-Sa'ib ibn Abi Kirdam, that he said: "I set out with my father on a journey, and with us was a flock of sheep. We descended into a valley," he said, "and a wolf came and took a lamb from the flock. My father stood up and said: 'O lord of the valley, we are under your protection!' When he said that, the wolf released the lamb, and the lamb returned to the flock, and it was not touched by a single bite."

If someone says: how can it be "men of the jinn," when the jinn are not called men? The answer: We say it is permissible by way of metaphor (majāz), and it has occurred in some reports of the Arabs in a narration that a group of jinn said: "We are people (unās) of the jinn." So if they may be called people, they may be called men.

As for His saying ﴿but they increased them in burden (rahaq)﴾, there are two opinions. The first: that mankind increased the jinn in rahaq, meaning in greatness in their own selves, as if when mankind sought refuge with the jinn, the jinn increased in greatness in their own estimation.

The second opinion: mankind increased in rahaq by seeking refuge with the jinn.

Its meaning is transgression and sin, as if when mankind sought refuge with the jinn and felt secure for themselves, they increased in disbelief, and thought that their security came from the jinn.

It was also said: rahaq means covering over the forbidden things (ghashayān lil-maḥārim).

It was also said: rahaq means the departure of the blamer (mufāraqat al-lā'im).

Al-A'shā said:

"Nothing benefits me except seeing her... Does a lover find healing if he has not been struck with rahaq?"

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And that they thought, as you thought, that Allah would never resurrect anyone﴾. In this verse there is evidence that among the jinn there were people who did not believe in the resurrection, just as there were among mankind.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 8:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And that we touched the heaven, but found it filled with a strong guard and meteors﴾. That is: filled with a guard of angels.

And His words: ﴿meteors﴾ are the plural of shihab (a meteor), which is a piece of fire. We have already mentioned earlier the manner in which the devils steal hearing from the heaven: they would hear a word and add to it ten [lies], and then convey it to the soothsayers (kahin, pl. kuhhan). When the time of the Prophet came, the heaven was guarded, and the devils were pelted with meteors.

If someone says: this matter was well known before the Messenger, namely the falling of stars, and the poets of the Jahiliyyah mentioned it in their poetry, and one of them said:

(Then it shot forth like a shining star, followed by ... a cloud of dust (it stirs up) you think it a tent-rope)

(He said it, and whoever meets him narrates it).

And if this was a known matter in the Jahiliyyah, what is the meaning of linking it to the prophethood of Muhammad, when you hold that it was a miracle for him and a foundation of his prophethood? The answer to this is in two respects. The first: this did not exist before; rather it occurred in the time of the Messenger's prophethood, and the poems are all falsely attributed to the Jahiliyyah, or they were composed after his birth, when his mission drew near.

As-Suddi mentioned that the first to notice the pelting with meteors was this tribe of Thaqif. They were greatly frightened and thought the Resurrection had drawn near, so they began to free slaves and let livestock loose. Ibn 'Abd Yalil said to them: "Do not hasten; look at the well-known stars and see whether they are in their places." They said: "They are in their places."

He said: "Then this is indeed for the matter of this man who has emerged in Makkah."

The second answer, which is the more correct, is that the pelting with meteors existed before, but when it came to the time of the Messenger it increased and grew stronger.

Ma'mar said: I said to az-Zuhri: "Was the pelting with meteors before the Messenger in the Jahiliyyah?" He said: "Yes, but when the time of the Messenger came it increased and intensified."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 9:

God Most High said: ﴿And we used to sit in some of its seats to listen.﴾ That is: seats for listening (istima').

And His saying: ﴿Whoever now listens will find for himself a watching flame.﴾ That is: he will find a shooting star lying in wait for him, to be hurled at him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾. That is: whether righteousness is intended for them in that, or corruption, or good, or evil.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 11:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those who are otherwise﴾. That is: other than that.

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: Among the jinn there are Qadariyya (adherents of free will), Murji'a (those who postpone judgment), Rafidha (Rafidites), Khawarij (Kharijites), and other sects. Among them are the disobedient, the obedient, and the reformers, and others among the believers and the disbelievers.

And His words: ﴿We were divided into diverse paths﴾. That is: possessing differing inclinations.

Qidadan (qiddadan) means: scattered, divided apart.

The poet said:

(Al-qabid al-basit al-hadi bi-ta'atihi ... fi fitnat al-nas idh ahwa'uhum qidad)

That is: scattered, divided apart.

Almighty Allah's saying: ﴿And we thought that we would never escape Allah on the earth﴾. The meaning of "thought" (ẓann) here is certainty (yaqīn), i.e., we were certain that we would never escape Him on the earth, meaning we would never elude Him, and He would not be unable to overtake us by seizing us.

And His saying: ﴿nor could we escape Him by flight﴾ — we have already explained it.

Allah's words, "And when we heard the guidance, we believed in it" (﴿وَأَنا لما سمعنَا الْهدى آمنا بِهِ﴾): i.e., in the guidance. The guidance is the Qur'an, because it guides people.

His words, "So whoever believes in his Lord will not fear loss (bakhsan) or burden (rahaqan)" (﴿فَمن يُؤمن بربه فَلَا يخَاف بخسا وَلَا رهقا﴾): i.e., a diminishing of his good deeds and no addition to his bad deeds.

It is also said: i.e., injustice (zulman).

The Exalted's statement: ﴿And among us are the Muslims, and among us are the unjust﴾, i.e., the transgressors, are the disbelievers.

It is said: aqsata (أقسط) means he was just, and qasata (قسط) means he acted unjustly.

So one who is just is muqsit (مقسط), and one who is unjust is qasit (قاسط).

Al-Farazdaq said:

(My people are those who killed the son of Hind by force, ʿAmr, and they acted unjustly toward al-Nuʿman.)

That is, they acted tyrannically (jaraw).

And His statement: ﴿So whoever has embraced Islam, those have sought out right guidance﴾, i.e., they sought out guidance (rushd) and aimed for it (tawakhkhaw).

Al-mutaharri (المتحري) and al-mutawakhkhi (المتوخي) have the same meaning.
"And His saying: ﴿As for the deviators, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾ That is: the disbelievers. And it is in the sense of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Its fuel is people and stones.﴾"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 16:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And if they had remained steadfast upon the way﴾. Regarding "the way" (al-tariqah) there are two opinions. The first is that it is faith (al-iman). This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, Ikrimah and a group, and it has the same meaning as the words of the Most High: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened up for them blessings from the heaven and the earth, but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn.﴾

The second opinion is that "the way" here is the way of disbelief and misguidance. This is the view of Abu Mujlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd from among the Successors (al-tabi'un), and it is the view of al-Farra' and a group. It has the same meaning as the words of the Most High: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses﴾, and so on.

Thus, their persistence in disbelief is made the cause for the expansion of blessings upon them. Likewise is the words of the Most High: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything﴾, and so on. Its meaning: the gates of everything of good things and blessings.

They said: The first opinion is more preferable, because it defines "the way" with the definite article (alif and lam), so it refers to the well-known, familiar way in the Shari'ah, which is faith.

As for His words: ﴿We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾, meaning: plentiful.

The Arabs say: "A galloping horse (faras ghaydaq)" when it is much running and wide-strided.

Its meaning: We would have increased for them wealth and provision, because abundance of water is a cause of abundance of wealth.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 17:

And His saying: ﴿That We may test them therein﴾, meaning: That We may try them therein and examine them therein.

.

From this verse, those who said that the meaning of "al-tariqah" (the path) is disbelief and misguidance drew their evidence, because He said: ﴿And that We may test them therein﴾. This does not necessarily follow for those who hold the first view, because abundance of blessings is a trial (fitnah) for believers and disbelievers alike.

And His saying: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord﴾, meaning: turns away from faith in his Lord, ﴿He will make him undergo a painful torment (sa'adan)﴾, meaning: arduous (shaqqan).

The arduous torment is the Fire, and its meaning is: He will cause him to enter the Fire.

From this is the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Nothing has ever made me toil (ta'addada) as much as the marriage sermon (khutbat al-nikah) has made me toil."

That is, it was arduous for me.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that His saying ﴿sa'adan﴾ is a mountain in Hell.

It was also said: it is a rock of fire that he is compelled to climb, and when he climbs it, he falls into the lowest level (al-darak al-asfal) of Hell.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 18:

God Most High says: ﴿And the mosques belong to God, so do not invoke anyone alongside God.﴾ The readers (qurra') agreed on opening the alif in this verse. The reason for the accusative (naṣb) is that its meaning is: "and because the mosques belong to God," then the lām was dropped, so the alif took the accusative.

It was also said: it is in the accusative because its meaning is: "It has been revealed to me that the mosques belong to God." The occasion of revelation of this verse is that the jinn said to the Prophet: "We wish to pray with you, so how shall we do it, when we are far from you?" So God Most High revealed His words: ﴿And the mosques belong to God﴾. Its meaning is: that if you pray, your purpose is achieved through the worship of God Most High, so do not associate anyone with Him, and this is the meaning of His words: ﴿so do not invoke anyone alongside God﴾. It is also said that it is the beginning of a new statement.

The meaning is: the Jews and the Christians associate others with God in their churches (biya') and monasteries (sawami'), and likewise the polytheists in the worship of idols. So you, O believers, know that prayers, prostrations and mosques are all for God, so do not associate anyone with Him.

Regarding "al-masajid" (the mosques) there are several views. The first: they mean prostrations (sujud), being the plural of masjid. It is said: "sajadtu sujudan wa masjadan," and the meaning is that prostration belongs to God, i.e., He is the one deserving of prostration.

The second view: the mosques are the built places prepared for prayer, being the plural of masjid. The meaning of His words ﴿for God﴾ is the negation of ownership over them by anyone else, or its meaning is the command to sincerely direct worship therein to God.

The third view: the mosques are the body parts on which a person prostrates: the forehead, the hands, the knees and the feet. The meaning is that it is not fitting to prostrate on these limbs except for God.

It has been related that Ibn 'Abbas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I have been commanded to prostrate on seven bones, and not to tuck up a garment or hair."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 19:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up﴾. Whoever reads it with a kasra (wa-annahu, "and indeed"), it refers to the speech of the jinn, and its meaning is: the jinn said, ﴿and indeed He﴾. It is also said that it refers to the speech of Allah, i.e., Allah the Exalted said: "And indeed, when the servant of Allah stood up." Whoever reads it with a fatha (wa-annahu), its meaning is: it was revealed to me that when the servant of Allah stood up.

According to the first view, His words ﴿they were almost upon him a compact mass﴾ refer to the Companions of the Prophet, and "the servant of Allah" is the Messenger. The meaning is that when the jinn saw the Prophet and his Companions behind him and witnessed their obedience to him, they said: "They were almost upon him a compact mass," i.e., some of them were piling upon others out of their eagerness to obey.

According to the second view, the meaning is that Allah the Exalted related of the jinn that when the Messenger recited the Qur'an to them, meaning to the jinn, ﴿they were almost upon him a compact mass﴾, i.e., upon the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, meaning some of them were piling upon others out of their love for listening to his recitation and hearing it.

It is also said that the Messenger was leading them in prayer and they crowded around him, and some of them nearly piled upon others.

In some tafsirs: "They nearly fell upon him."

As for the reading with fatha, His words ﴿they were almost upon him a compact mass﴾ also refer to the jinn, and the view that the reference is to the jinn is the more apparent of the two views.

From the root "lubd" they said: "talabbada al-qawm" (the people gathered together) when they assembled, and from it comes "libd" (a felt mat), because some of it is upon other parts.

It is also said: ﴿they were almost upon him a compact mass﴾, meaning the jinn and mankind gathered together and massed to extinguish the light of Allah when the Messenger stood calling upon Him, i.e., calling upon Allah. It was also read as "lubadan," meaning many.

Al-Lubad is also the name of another vulture of the vultures of (Nu'man) ibn 'Ad, and he lived seven hundred years.

It is said in the proverb: "Lubad has lingered too long over a term."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 20:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: I only call upon my Lord﴾. It is also read: "Qala innama ad'u rabbi" (He said: I only call upon my Lord). In the tafsir (exegesis) it is reported that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said to the Prophet: "You have come with a great matter, you have opposed the religion of your forefathers, and the Arabs will not agree with you on this, so return to the religion of your forefathers." Then God, the Exalted, revealed His saying: ﴿Say: I only call upon my Lord﴾, meaning: I make my Lord singular (in worship), ﴿and I do not associate with Him anyone﴾, meaning: I do not take anyone along with Him.

It is also said: this was spoken to the jinn, and it is in sequence with what preceded.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance.﴾ He means: I do not possess that by myself; rather, it is from God, may He be exalted, and by His help and His enabling success.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 22:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, none can protect me from Allah, and I will not find any refuge other than Him﴾. It is related that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said to him: "Return to the religion of your fathers, and do not fear anyone, for we will protect you and defend you." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Say: Indeed, none can protect me from Allah﴾, meaning: none can help me or defend me from the punishment of Allah.

It is also said that this is an address to the jinn, in sequence with what came before.

Abu al-Jawza' related from Ibn 'Abbas that Ibn Mas'ud went out with the Prophet on the night of the jinn, and the jinn crowded around the Prophet and swarmed upon him. One of them, called Wardan, said: "O Muhammad, do not fear, for I will protect you from them." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Say: Indeed, none can protect me from Allah﴾.

As for His words: ﴿And I will not find any refuge other than Him﴾, meaning: a place of shelter (multaja').

It is also said: a place of escape (mahrab).

It is said: a place of turning aside (mata'arraja').

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 23:

And His saying: ﴿Except a message from Allah﴾, meaning: I possess none of the harm or the right guidance, except that I convey the message of my Lord. That is, there is in my hand nothing but this, and this conveying (al-tabligh).

It has also been said: ﴿harm or right guidance﴾, meaning: I cannot repel harm from you, nor bring you any good; there is in my hand nothing except that I convey the message of my Lord.

And His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾, meaning: perpetually.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when they see that which they are promised﴾, meaning: the Resurrection. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others.

It is also said: it refers to the punishment in this world. This was said by Qatadah and others.

As for His saying: ﴿Then they will know who is weaker in helper and fewer in number﴾, meaning: who has fewer soldiers and helpers.

It is also said: the meaning of His saying ﴿and fewer in number﴾ is: on the Day of Resurrection.

In the exegesis (tafsir) it is related that Allah, exalted is He, gives the believers wives, youths (wildan) and maidens (huur), and attendants (qahärima), and that their number increases and exceeds the people of a great city in the lands of this world. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then they will know who is weaker in helper and fewer in number﴾, for the polytheists used to reproach the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers for having few helpers and few in number. So He said: ﴿Then they will know who is weaker in helper and fewer in number﴾, meaning: on the Day of Resurrection, and when each one has reached his station.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 25:

The words of the Most High, ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will appoint for it a term (amad)﴾. That is: a period (muddah) and a limit (ghayah). The meaning is: I do not know whether He will hasten the punishment for you or delay it, and whether He will hasten for you a period and a respite.

It is related that the polytheists used to urge him to hasten the punishment, saying: "Until when will you threaten us with the punishment? Where is the punishment?" So God the Most High commanded him to leave that matter to God the Most High, and to say: "It is in the hand of God, not in my hand."
Divine saying, the Exalted: ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, so He does not reveal His unseen to anyone.﴾ That is: He is the Knower of the unseen, so He does not reveal His unseen to anyone.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 27:

﴿Except for whomever He has approved of among the messengers﴾, for indeed He causes him to know of His unseen by what He sends down to him of signs and clear proofs.

And His saying: ﴿For indeed He sends forth before him and behind him a guard﴾, meaning: He makes before him and behind him ﴿a guard﴾, meaning: protectors.

Sufyan narrated from Mansur from Ibrahim, who said: "They are angels who guard him."

It is mentioned in tafsir that Allah Most High never sent down revelation from the heaven except that with it were angels guarding it.

If someone says: From what do they protect and guard it? The answer is: the protection and guarding are due to the great importance of the revelation and its exalted status in hearts, not by way of need for guarding and guardians.

It is said: the protection and guarding are against those who eavesdrop on the heavens, lest they steal something of that and throw it to the soothsayers (kahin, pl. kuhhan).

It has been reported in the traditions: "When Allah Most High sent down Surah al-An'am, He sent with it seventy thousand angels guarding it."

In the verse there is evidence that whoever speaks about the stars concerning something and claims knowledge of the unseen by way of them, then he is a disbeliever in the Qur'an.

Some of them said: the diviners by pebbles (tarq), the idols (jibt), and the soothsayers (kahin) are all misguided, and they point toward the unseen only from behind it.

It has been reported in the traditions: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade looking into the stars (nujum)."

The meaning is looking into them in order to speak of the unseen through them. As for looking into them for guidance, or for reflection, or for knowing the qibla, and what is similar to that, it is absolutely permissible.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 72, verse 28:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿That He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾. It was also read as "risalata Rabbihim" (the messages of their Lord, in the singular), and risala is the singular of risalat (messages).

Opinions have differed concerning His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿That He may know﴾. One of the opinions is that its meaning is: that Muhammad may know that the messengers who were before him had conveyed the messages of their Lord in accordance with what was sent down to them.

The second opinion: that it refers to the jinn.

It was read as: "That the jinn may know that the messengers had conveyed the messages of their Lord in accordance with what was sent down to them."

The third opinion: that it means "That the believers may know."

The fourth opinion: that it means "That Allah may know." This was related by al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) and others.

If someone says: what is the meaning of His saying "That Allah may know", when He knows things before they come into being and exist? The answer: we have already explained the answer in many places earlier.

It has also been said: that Allah, the Exalted, may know, in the sense of witnessing and existence, that the messengers had conveyed the messages of their Lord, although He had known this unseen beforehand.

As for His saying: ﴿And He encompasses what is with them﴾, meaning: His knowledge encompasses what is with them.

As for His saying: ﴿And He has enumerated everything in number﴾, meaning: and He has counted every thing as a counted quantity.

It is said: "He counted everything in number," and this is in the sense that nothing is hidden from Allah, whether little or much, great or minute.

And Allah knows best.
